newsitem.title: UK: Robust Dixons' sales suggest UK windfall spending.
newsitem.headline: Robust Dixons' sales suggest UK windfall spending.

text.p: Bumper trading figures out on Wednesday from Britain's biggest electrical retailer point to a spending spree by Britons flush with windfall cash from building society flotations.
But analysts said they needed more data evidence covering the key months of June and July before they can forecast the full impact of cash handouts on the economy.
Retailer Dixons announced a 32 percent overall rise in retail division sales over the last nine weeks.

"The useful thing about the comments from Dixons is that it is precisely this sort of business that would benefit if consumers were spending their windfalls," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Co-operative Bank.
Most economists agree that any increased spending triggered by windfall cash will find its way to holidays, cars and big ticket consumer durables, such as electrical items, Dixons' stock-in-trade.
"The problem is in extending what Dixons has said about its business to the rest of the economy. It is too small a sample and still too soon to say how the economy will be affected," said Snowball.
Dixons said windfall payments boosted its sales of personal computers and major household appliances.
"It would be naive of us to believe that there wasn't an impact on these current trading numbers because this amount of money is coming into the consumer economy," said chief executive John Clare.
Like-for-like sales rose by 17 percent in the period against expectations of a single-figure increase.
Dixons' results came just hours before the Bank of England's monetary policy committee met to discuss interest rates.

The Bank is widely expected to raise the 6.5 percent base rate when it makes its announcement at midday on Thursday to try and cool consumer spending, already strong and set to be boosted by the windfalls.
Economists estimate around 35 billion pounds will be pumped into the economy this year as a result of the spate of building society flotations.
Anecdotal evidence and data covering spending patterns in June and July will be crucial as the lion's share of this year's payments will be made in these two months.

Retail sales figures for June will be released on July 21. May's figures showed a sharp rise of 1.1 percent on the month, leading some economists to speculate that consumers were spending in advance of receiving the cash, but most said it was too soon to say.
Halifax Plc paid out a total of 17 billion pounds and Norwich Union 4.0 billion in June, while earlier this week Woolwich Plc paid out around 5.5 billion pounds.
But while economists roughly agree on the total amount of cash due to be paid out to building society members during the year, forecasts on the proportion likely to be spent vary dramatically.

The Bank of England's forecast is at the bottom end of expectations at 5.0 percent. The Treasury's at 15 percent is in the middle, with some independent economists forecasting as much as 25 percent will be spent.
Stephen Radley, economist at the Henley Centre for Forecasting, an independent firm of consultants, forecasts any amount up to 25 percent could be spent and the Bank's forecast is too low.
"I think the Bank is far too cautious. It believes people only respond to a permanent change in wealth."
But he said the Bank is right to suppose the bulk of the cash will be saved.
"There is a definite bias to people in their late forties or older in the pattern of building society membership, and this group tend to be savers."
Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers, said the background of higher salaries and rising consumer confidence further complicated the picture.
"Retail sales were certainly strong in May, but revisions to back data showed spending was much higher in the first quarter, long before we were in windfall territory."
He forecasts around 5.0 percent of the total windfalls will be spent, but acknowledges the risks are firmly on the upside.
"That forecast is deduced from the permanent gain in income if the windfall is invested. There is no real downside risk to that forecast, it's all on the upside." --LONDON NEWSROOM ++44 171 542 7717
